questions.q: What does `thermal_relaxation_error` model, that `depolarizing_error` does not?
options: Classical bit-flip errors in a measurement device
Real T1 energy relaxation and T2 dephasing as a function of gate duration
Errors caused only by cosmic rays
A gate that always succeeds perfectly
questions.explain: thermal_relaxation_error is physically grounded in real T1 (energy relaxation) and T2 (dephasing) decoherence, scaled by how long the gate takes to execute, whereas depolarizing_error is a simpler stand-in that replaces a gate with a random Pauli error with some probability.

questions.q: A qubit is prepared in |0⟩ with no gates applied, then a 2% bit-flip-style error channel is injected before measurement. Under zero shot noise, what are the true probabilities P(0) and P(1)?
questions.explain: With no noise, the qubit would measure 0 with probability 1.0 every time. Injecting a 2% error channel on top of that gives true probabilities P(0)=0.98 and P(1)=0.02.

questions.q: A seeded 1024-shot run of that same 2%-error circuit returns `{'0': 1000, '1': 24}`, an observed error rate of about 2.34% instead of exactly 2.00%. What best explains the gap?
options: The noise model is broken and needs to be rebuilt
Statistical shot noise from a finite number of samples, layered on top of the true injected error rate
Qiskit Aer always rounds error rates up
The 'x' gate was applied to the wrong qubit
questions.explain: The injected error sets a true 2% probability, but any finite number of shots is a statistical sample of that probability and will wobble around it due to shot noise — a separate source of imperfection from the injected hardware error itself.

questions.q: What does `readout_error` specifically model, that distinguishes it from a gate-level error channel like `depolarizing_error`?
options: An error in how the circuit is drawn
A misreporting of the measurement outcome itself, independent of whether the quantum state was correct
An error that can never be corrected
A delay in job queueing on real hardware
questions.explain: readout_error models the classical measurement/readout hardware misreporting the outcome — a qubit truly in state 0 is sometimes read as 1 and vice versa — which is a different failure mode from a gate corrupting the underlying quantum state.

questions.q: Why would you use `NoiseModel.from_backend(backend)` instead of hand-building a noise model with `pauli_error`?
options: It runs faster than any hand-built model
It pulls the backend's actual live calibrated noise profile, giving a more realistic preview before spending real hardware queue time
It removes all noise from the simulation
It is required before any circuit can be transpiled
questions.explain: from_backend() builds a noise model from a real device's current measured gate errors, T1/T2 times, and readout errors, which is far more representative of real behavior than a hand-picked illustrative value, and is valuable for testing before using real hardware quota.
